paper_title: PremiseCheck: Efficient Fact-Checking of Human and AI Peer Reviews

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Peer review is under strain from the growth of submissions, and review comments written by humans or AI can misstate what a paper says. We introduce ReviewFact, a benchmark that labels such factual errors in review comments under one definition across NLP, machine learning, and the natural sciences, and that measures cost and latency alongside accuracy. A frontier LLM checks comments well but must read the whole paper for each check, while cheap decision models, which score whether a statement holds in a text, fall far short on whole comments that mix several implicit assertions. PremiseCheck is a framework that combines the two. An LLM rewrites each comment as explicit premises without reading the paper, and a decision model checks each premise against the paper. When each comment is checked on its own, PremiseCheck reaches accuracy comparable to GPT-5.5 across all three fields at about half its cost, and on NLP reviews at a quarter of its cost and less than half its latency.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: The number of research papers has grown explosively in recent years, and reviewing them now places heavy burden on the scientific community (Shah, 2022; Kuznetsov et al., 2024; Kim et al., 2025). review comment is useful only if what it says about the paper is true, yet factual errors appear regularly in both human-written and AI-written comments (Du et al., 2024; Ryu et al., 2025; Kim et al., 2026), and AI systems now help write growing share of reviews (Liang et al., 2024a; Thakkar et al., 2025; Biswas et al., 2026). Such errors mislead authors and distort decisions, and at the present scale they can no longer be caught by hand. An area chair cannot reread each paper to check every comment, and an author can correct an error only in the rebuttal. We therefore study the fact-checking of review comments as task of its own. Given paper and one comment from review of it, system scores how likely the comment says something that the paper does not support. Errors of judgment, such as whether concern matters, are out of scope. Existing expert annotations of review comments label factual errors inconsistently, if at all. Our benchmark, ReviewFact, builds on them (Du et al., 2024; Ryu et al., 2025; Kim et al., 2026) and labels every comment under one definition of factual error. Because system 1 Figure 1 Three ways to check review comment, shown on real comment from ReviewFact. AUROC, cost, and time are measured on the NLP reviews of ReviewFact, with cost relative to the LLM-only row, which is the reference in our experiments. The LLM is GPT-5.5 and the decision model is Jev. would run on every comment of every review, ReviewFact evaluates cost and latency together with accuracy. The task is hard because each error is something an expert reviewer overlooked or misread, and the evidence against it may lie anywhere in long paper. comment also rarely states its claim directly, as question such as Did the authors test other models? presupposes that the paper does not test them. When each comment is checked on its own, existing systems are either accurate or cheap, but not both. frontier LLM that judges each comment on its own (Zheng et al., 2023; Ryu et al., 2025; Thakkar et al., 2025) must reread the full paper for every comment, cost that multiplies across tens of thousands of reviews. Instead of generating text, decision model such as Jev returns the probability that statement holds in document, typically within fraction of second and at negligible cost (Almeida, 2026; TypeSafe AI, 2026). Yet on whole comments, Jev performs at chance level on the NLP reviews and well below an LLM on the other two parts. review comment mixes several assertions, many implicit, whereas decision model, like single-claim fact-checkers (Laban et al., 2022; Zha et al., 2023; Tang et al., 2024), is reliable only on explicit, self-contained claims. On single premises that human annotators wrote out from review comments, however, Jev is as accurate as GPT-5.5 (Appendix D.1). Our key insight is that understanding what comment asserts needs an LLM but not the paper, whereas reading the paper is the expensive part and decision model can do it once the assertions are explicit. PremiseCheck is framework that combines the two kinds of models. An LLM rewrites each comment as few explicit premises without reading the paper (Min et al., 2023; Wei et al., 2024; Ryu et al., 2025). decision model then decides how to check each premise and verifies it against the paper, and the comment receives the score of its weakest premise. Figure 1 contrasts PremiseCheck with either kind of model alone. With medium-reasoning decomposer, PremiseCheck stays within 0.3 AUROC points of holistic GPT-5.5 or above it on every part of ReviewFact at about half its cost, and on the NLP reviews decomposer without reasoning cuts the cost to quarter while remaining non-inferior. The accuracy comes from decomposition rather than from one model, since four decision models from different providers, including the open-weight Kev-27B, come within one point of holistic GPT-5.5 as verifiers. Our contributions are as follows. We propose PremiseCheck, framework that turns the verification of review comment into decision problems, combining the flexibility of an LLM with the efficiency of decision model. decision model checks each premise against the paper or against general knowledge and asks several phrasings of its question in one call. We define the task of fact-checking single review comments and build ReviewFact, benchmark that labels factual errors in human-written and AI-written review comments across NLP, machine learning, and the natural sciences and measures cost and latency alongside accuracy. ReviewFact holds 9,267 comments on 217 papers. We validate PremiseCheck on all three parts of ReviewFact, where it checks each comment on its own with accuracy comparable to GPT-5.5 at fraction of its cost. cascade costs more than PremiseCheck yet is less accurate on every part.

As LLMs write reviews and critique human ones (Liang et al., 2024b; D’Arcy et al., 2024; Zhu et al., 2025;

2024), ReviewScore (Ryu et al., 2025), PeerReview Bench (Kim et al., 2026), and ClaimCheck (Ou et al.,
2025) annotate review comments against the paper. These datasets serve broader goals and label factual
errors inconsistently, if at all, whereas ReviewFact applies one definition across three fields and also scores
cost and latency. Systems that generate reviews aim to write better comments, whereas PremiseCheck checks
comments that have already been written.

3.2 Labels from Expert Annotations
ReviewFact adds no new comments or papers. It reuses expert judgments of review comments from one
dataset per field, ReviewCritique for NLP, ReviewScore for machine learning, and PeerReview Bench for the

all three parts, which we call the NLP, machine learning, and natural-science reviews, and AI reviewers also
wrote comments in the NLP and natural-science reviews. Each dataset was built for a broader goal, so we
map its annotations to our label and leave out comments outside the task, following the rules in Appendix A.1.

sections.content: Human verification. Many comments that the PeerReview Bench experts judged incorrect are errors of judgment rather than factual errors, so GPT-5.5 decides from the experts rationale whether the error is factual. Two of the authors independently repeat this decision on the 178 comments that have rationale, without seeing the GPT-5.5 labels or each others labels (Appendix A.2). The two annotators agree with Cohens κ of 0.70, and GPT-5.5 agrees with them with κ of 0.76 and 0.77, so we keep the GPT-5.5 labels. With the labels of the annotators instead, the difference between PremiseCheck and holistic GPT-5.5 on these reviews ranges from 3.7 to +2.7 and is never significant, so the GPT-5.5 labels do not favor the GPT-5.5 reference.

sections.title: 3.3 Statistics
sections.content: Figure 3 summarizes the 9,267 comments on 217 papers. Factual errors are rare, 4.8% of the NLP comments and 2.5% of the natural-science comments, so system spends most of its calls on correct comments and its cost matters. The machine learning reviews have higher share of errors because they keep only arguments, that is, comments that give reasons for conclusion. ReviewScore rates the premises of arguments only, so we leave out its claims and questions (Appendix A.1). The median comment has 17, 48, and 70 words, and the median paper has 8.5k, 9.1k, and 14.4k tokens in the NLP, machine learning, and natural-science reviews. comment is thus short compared with the paper it refers to, so system that reads the paper for every comment spends almost all of its input on the paper.

sections.title: 5 Experimental Setup
sections.content: Models. Our implementation of PremiseCheck uses GPT-5.5 as the decomposer and Jev as the decision model, which reads the paper truncated to 24k tokens.1 On the machine learning and natural-science reviews, the decomposer uses the prompt variants of Appendix B.1. Our main setting scores each comment on its own, as an assistant would check comment as soon as the reviewer writes it, before the rest of the review exists. Checking all comments of finished review together is different setting, which we evaluate in 8.1. Appendix B.3 gives the prices of the LLMs. Baselines. Holistic judgment gives model the paper and the comment and asks for the probability that the comments main criticism is factually correct. We run it with GPT-5.5 at medium, low, and no reasoning, with GPT-5.4-mini, and with Jev. The reference system is holistic GPT-5.5 at medium reasoning. cascade scores all comments with holistic Jev and sends the 70% it finds most suspicious to holistic GPT-5.5. Metrics. We call system non-inferior to the reference when the lower bound of the 95% interval for the paired AUROC difference, from bootstrap over papers with 2,000 resamples, is above 3, margin we fixed before running the experiments. Holistic judgment reads the same paper for every comment, so we count its repeated input at the cached price, which favors the baseline.

sections.title: 9 Conclusion
sections.content: Fact-checking review comments does not require frontier LLM to read the paper for every comment. ReviewFact labels factual errors in review comments under one definition across three fields. In PremiseCheck, an LLM only rewrites each comment as explicit premises, and cheap decision model checks them against the paper. When each comment is checked on its own, this division of labor reaches accuracy comparable to GPT-5.5 on every part of ReviewFact at fraction of its cost. This result does not hinge on one model. Decision models from several providers can verify the premises, and on the NLP reviews, LLMs much cheaper than GPT-5.5, or GPT-5.5 without reasoning, can write them. PremiseCheck can support peer review at two points. While reviewer writes, it can check each comment as soon as the comment is written, which is the setting of our main experiments. Once review is finished, an area chair or an author can check all its comments together, where fusing PremiseCheck with holistic GPT-5.5 gives the best accuracy. In both cases, PremiseCheck is meant to flag few comments for person and show the premise that the paper appears to refute, so that the person can check that one claim instead of rereading the paper. Several directions remain open. Most false alarms on the NLP reviews arise in decomposition, so decomposer that stays closer to what the reviewer said is natural next step. Errors of judgment, such as an unimportant concern or an unreasonable request, lie outside PremiseCheck and call for different methods. Finally, ReviewFact can measure future checkers on accuracy, cost, and latency together, and further open-weight decision models can be tested within the same framework.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: PremiseCheck targets factual errors about the paper, that is, comments that can be checked against what the paper states. comment can also be wrong in its judgment, for example about the importance of concern or the novelty of the work (7.4). Detecting such errors of judgment is direction for future work. Our main decision model, Jev, is served through an API. With the open-weight Kev-27B as the decision model, PremiseCheck reaches the same AUROC on the NLP reviews of ReviewFact (6.2). Testing further open decision models is left for future work.

sections.title: Ethical Considerations
sections.content: We use ReviewCritique, ReviewScore, and PeerReview Bench for research evaluation only. The license of ReviewCritique restricts it to research and evaluation, and we do not train any model on it. We release our code under the MIT license and the NLP and natural-science parts of ReviewFact under the licenses of ReviewCritique and PeerReview Bench, which allow evaluation but not training. ReviewScore states no license, so for the machine-learning part we release script that rebuilds it from the original data instead of the data itself. verifier that wrongly flags correct comment could unfairly discredit reviewer, and one that misses an error could lend false authority to wrong comment. PremiseCheck is meant to direct human attention to comments that may misstate the paper, not to replace the judgment of reviewers, area chairs, or authors.

sections.title: A Benchmark Details
sections.content: A.1 Source Annotations All labels of ReviewFact start from expert judgments in the three source datasets (3.2). In ReviewCritique (Du et al., 2024), 40 members of the NLP community, ReviewCritique (NLP reviews). each with multiple first-authored papers at top NLP venues, label every sentence of review as reliable or deficient and explain each deficiency. They read the paper, all reviews, the meta-review, and the author rebuttal before labeling. Two of them label each paper independently, and an expert with area-chair experience resolves disagreements. Each labeled unit of review is one comment in ReviewFact. Deficient comments carry fine-grained error types, four of which are the factual types of ReviewFact. Reliable comments are correct, and deficient comments with one of these four types are errors. We leave out other deficiencies, such as an unconvincing argument, comments that only summarize the paper or list its strengths, and comments of fewer than four words, mostly headers such as Weaknesses:. In ReviewScore (Ryu et al., 2025), 15 graduate students in ReviewScore (machine learning reviews). AI rate each premise of an automatically reconstructed argument on five-point factuality scale, and the median of three annotators is the final score. Following ReviewScore, an argument is an error when its lowest premise rating is below 3 and correct when it is above 3. We leave out arguments at exactly 3, as well as claims and questions, which have no premise ratings. 14 In PeerReview Bench (Kim et al., 2026), 45 scientists in PeerReview Bench (natural-science reviews). the physical, biological, and health sciences judge whether each comment on Nature-family paper is correct and may add written rationale. Comments judged correct are correct. Comments judged incorrect are errors only when the error is factual, as decided in Appendix A.2. A.2 Label Verification Human verification. Two of the authors repeat the GPT-5.5 decision of 3.2 on the 178 comments that PeerReview Bench experts judged incorrect with rationale. Each annotator sees the comment, the expert rationale, and the paper text, but not the GPT-5.5 label, and the two annotators see the comments in different random orders. The guidelines in Figure 13 define the three labels with the error types of ReviewCritique. Table 2 reports the agreement. Of the 38 comments with different labels, 17 are labeled factual by one annotator and judgment by the other, and 21 involve the unclear label. Each row is review comment that an expert annotator of PeerReview Bench judged Not Correct, with the experts rationale. Decide why the expert judged it incorrect, using the comment and the rationale. Open the paper only when the rationale is not enough to decide. Work alone, and do not discuss rows with the other annotator before both sheets are done. Choose exactly one label. factual: the comment says something about this paper that the paper does not support. Give the subtype. Misunderstanding: misreads what the paper does or claims. Neglect: says the paper lacks something that it clearly contains (an experiment, detail, discussion). Unstated statement: asserts something about the paper that has no basis in it. Inaccurate summary: misstates the content or contribution of the paper. judgment: the comment is wrong in its judgment, not its facts, for example about importance, scope, or novelty, an unreasonable request, being too harsh or overstated, or disagreement about field knowledge. An error about cited paper rather than this paper also counts as judgment. unclear: the rationale does not let you decide. When the rationale mainly says that the comment is too harsh or overstated but also mentions the papers content, choose judgment.
